1394.title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
1394.hook: a festival song about a king so good that the gods grew worried
1394.howItsDone: At Onam, families in Kerala remember Mahabali's reign with songs, flower designs at the door and a shared feast, and the Bhagavata Purana's account of Bali and Vamana is retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Kashmir: Herath, Shiva's great night, and the soaked walnuts carried door to door. Today, the far southwest.

When Maveli ruled the land, everyone was alike. That's the opening, in paraphrase, of a folk song sung in Kerala at Onam. It goes on: there was no theft and no cheating, not even a small lie. Nobody was in trouble, and nobody was afraid. It sounds like a children's daydream. But the king in the song isn't a god. He's an asura, from the side of the stories usually cast as the gods' rivals. And he was so good at being king that heaven itself got nervous.
screen: `A SONG ABOUT A GOOD KING` → `NO THEFT, NO LIES` → `A KING FROM THE OTHER SIDE`

segments.voice: Year one gave you Onam: a king's yearly homecoming. Here is the king. His name is Bali, and Kerala calls him Mahabali, great Bali, or Maveli for short. His story is told in the Bhagavata Purana. He's the grandson of Prahlada, the boy devotee who held to Vishnu through every danger. Bali is generous, devout and strong, and with the help of his teacher Shukra, he wins the three worlds, heaven included. The gods are pushed out. Their mother, Aditi, grieves for them and prays. And notice what the text does not say. It doesn't call Bali cruel. His problem isn't wickedness. The order of the worlds has been turned upside down, and a good man is sitting on a throne that isn't his. Vishnu answers Aditi's prayer by being born as her son, Vamana, a small brahmin boy. He walks to Bali's great sacrifice, where the king is giving gifts to anyone who asks. Bali welcomes him warmly: ask for anything, land, wealth, villages. And the boy asks for almost nothing. Only as much ground as he can cover in three of his own steps. Bali tells him it's a child's request, far too small. Today stops there, with the king's hand raised to give. Kerala's Onam is built around a king who lost his throne, and the song remembers him not as a loser but as a ruler worth longing for.

1395.title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
1395.hook: a teacher warns the king that the small boy is Vishnu, and the king keeps his promise anyway
1395.howItsDone: At Onam, Keralites retell how Mahabali kept his word to Vamana and offered his head for the third step, and the Bhagavata Purana's account of it is read and recited in the season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa began with Mahabali, the good asura king, and a small boy asking for three steps of ground.

The water pot is already tilted. In the old way of giving a gift, the giver pours water to seal the promise, and Bali is about to pour. Then his teacher, Shukra, pulls him aside. Shukra sees what the king doesn't: that small boy is Vishnu. Give him three steps and he will take everything you have. Take your word back, he says. Here, even a teacher thinks a lie would be wiser. Today, what a good king does with a promise that's about to cost him the world.
screen: `THE WATER POT TILTED` → `SHUKRA'S WARNING` → `A PROMISE THAT WILL COST`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana gives Shukra a strong case. He tells Bali that this boy is Vishnu in disguise, and that the gift will strip him of everything. He even argues that in some moments, an untrue word is allowed. It's a teacher's counsel, and it isn't foolish. Bali hears him out, and refuses. In paraphrase, he says: I am Prahlada's grandson. I have said I will give. I will not take it back. And the text puts a striking line in his mouth: the earth can carry any weight except the weight of a liar. So Bali pours the water. Shukra, angry, curses him to lose his fortune. Then the small boy begins to grow, past the sacrifice, past the trees, past the sky, until he holds the worlds inside his body. With one step he covers the earth. With the second, the heavens. There's nowhere left for the third. Bali's own soldiers rush at the giant, and Bali stops them. He is bound with ropes. Then Vamana asks, in effect: you promised three steps, and I've taken two; where does the third one go? And Bali answers: put it on my head. He has lost his kingdom, his treasure, his freedom. The one thing he refuses to lose is his word, and he gives the last of himself, his own head, to keep it.
screen: `SHUKRA: TAKE YOUR WORD BACK` · `BALI: I WILL NOT` · `TWO STEPS COVER EVERYTHING` · `THE THIRD STEP ON HIS HEAD`

segments.voice: Hold one promise you've made that's still open, to a friend, a child, a parent, yourself, the way Bali held the water pot, without judging it yet. Ask quietly what keeping it would cost, and what breaking it would cost. Then breathe out and let your head bow a little, the way Bali bowed his.

1396.title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
1396.hook: a king who lost everything gets a guard at his door, and a visit home that Kerala gets ready for
1396.howItsDone: At Onam, families in Kerala lay a pookalam of flower petals at the door, wear new clothes and share the sadya, a feast served on a banana leaf, to welcome Mahabali on his visit to his people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa brought Bali's choice: warned by his teacher, he kept his word and offered his head for the third step.

Where do you send a king who has just lost the three worlds? Bali was left bound, his head under the foot of the giant Vamana. A story could end there, with the proud one humbled. The Bhagavata Purana doesn't. And Kerala doesn't either. On an Onam morning in Kerala, someone is on their knees at the front door, laying flower petals into a circle, ring by ring. In the way Kerala tells it, they're getting ready for a guest.
screen: `BALI BOUND` → `FLOWERS BEFORE DAWN` → `READY FOR A GUEST`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata, Bali's grandfather Prahlada arrives, and Bali's wife pleads for him. And Vishnu explains himself. Taking a person's wealth, he says, can be a kind of grace, because it frees them. Then he gives Bali a new home, a realm under the earth called Sutala, a place of comfort and peace. And he makes a startling promise: he will be there himself, standing at Bali's door with his mace in his hand, guarding him. The god who took the worlds becomes the doorkeeper of the king who gave them. Here Kerala adds what the Bhagavata doesn't say. Tradition in Kerala says Bali asked for one more thing: to come back and see his people once a year. Onam is that visit. The king who once made the land fair comes up to look at it again. So people get ready the way you'd get ready for someone you love. The flower carpet at the door is the pookalam. The great meal, the sadya, is served on a banana leaf, with dish after dish set out in its place, and families sit down together to eat it. New clothes, games, boat races on the rivers, songs. Not because a god demands it, but because a beloved king is coming to see whether his people are still well. Losing the throne wasn't the end of Bali. It's the reason he's remembered.
screen: `SUTALA: A NEW HOME FOR BALI` · `VISHNU GUARDS BALI'S DOOR` · `ONE VISIT HOME A YEAR` · `FLOWERS, A FEAST, A WELCOME`

segments.voice: With each slow breath, lay down one ring of petals, the way a pookalam is built from the center out: one ring for the people in your home, one for your street, one for someone you haven't seen in a long time. Keep going, ring by ring, until the circle feels wide enough, then rest in the middle of it.
Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, Bali's reward: Vishnu guards his door, and Kerala welcomes him home each Onam with flowers and a feast. Today's word.

1397.title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
1397.hook: a childless king out hunting hears a baby crying by the river, a small bell at its neck
1397.howItsDone: Devotees of Ayyappa tell how he was born of Shiva and Vishnu as Mohini, found as a baby by the Pampa river and raised by the king of Pandalam, and the Pandalam royal family keeps a special place in his worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa gave Bali his reward: Vishnu at his door, and a flower welcome every Onam. Today the same title turns from Onam to Ayyappa, the god of a forest hill.

A crying sound, thin and high, somewhere near the river. The king of Pandalam is out hunting in the forest, and he stops his horse to listen. It isn't a bird. He follows the sound down to the bank of the Pampa, and there, alone on the ground, is a baby boy, bright as a lamp, with a small bell tied around his neck. No mother. No hut. No one. And the king has no children of his own.
screen: `A CRY BY THE RIVER` → `A BABY WITH A BELL` → `A KING WITH NO CHILDREN`

segments.voice: In the story as it's told in Kerala, a demoness named Mahishi has won a boon that makes her almost impossible to defeat. Only a son born of Shiva and Vishnu together could overcome her, and that sounds like a riddle with no answer. Here's the answer. Vishnu once took the form of Mohini, an enchanting woman, and from Shiva and Mohini a child is born. So Ayyappa is called Hariharaputra, the son of Hari and Hara: Hari is a name of Vishnu, and Hara a name of Shiva. In one small boy, the worship of Shiva and the worship of Vishnu meet. The child is left by the river Pampa with a bell at his neck. The king of Pandalam finds him and longs to keep him. In the telling, a holy man appears and tells the king: take him home, raise him as your son, and the truth will come out in time. So the king carries him back to the palace, and they call him Manikandan, which the story explains as the one with the bell at his throat. The boy who is the son of two gods grows up as an adopted child in a human family, loved by a father who doesn't fully know who he is. Ayyappa's story will soon become a story of a pilgrimage up a forest hill. But it starts with a man who hears a cry and turns his horse toward it.

1398.title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
1398.hook: a queen's strange illness, a cure no one could fetch, and a boy who rides home on a tigress
1398.howItsDone: Ayyappa is often shown seated on or beside a tiger, and devotees retell how Manikandan went into the forest for tiger's milk and came home riding a tigress.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa: a baby with a bell at his neck, found by the Pampa river and raised by the king of Pandalam as Manikandan.

The prescription is impossible on purpose. The queen of Pandalam lies in a darkened room, clutching her head. The palace physician bows and gives his verdict: only one cure will work, the milk of a tigress. The room goes silent. Nobody walks into the forest and milks a tiger, and the physician knows it. Because the illness, in the story, isn't real. It's a plan to send someone into the forest who isn't supposed to come back. Today, the boy who went anyway.
screen: `AN IMPOSSIBLE CURE` → `THE MILK OF A TIGRESS` → `AN ILLNESS THAT ISN'T REAL`

segments.voice: In the telling, after the king adopts Manikandan, the queen has a son of her own. A scheming minister whispers to her that the adopted boy will take the throne from her child. Afraid, she agrees to pretend to be ill, and the physician is in on it. It's an old human fear, the kind that makes ordinary people do things they later regret. Manikandan is still young. He hears what the cure is, and he offers to go. The king begs him not to. The boy goes anyway, alone, into the forest, with a bundle of food for the road. The story doesn't make him angry, and it doesn't make him suspicious. He simply goes to fetch what his mother says she needs. In the forest, tradition says, Manikandan meets the demoness Mahishi and overcomes her, which was why he was born. Then he comes home, not with a pot of milk, but riding on a tigress, with a band of tigers walking behind him. In some tellings the tigers are gods in disguise. The palace gate is full of terrified people. The queen and the minister, seeing him, understand what they've done, and fall at his feet asking forgiveness. And the king finally understands who his son is. The story puts its weight not on punishment for the plotters, but on what the boy does with their plot: he turns a trap into an errand of care, and comes back with more than they asked for.

1399.hook: on the climb to Sabarimala, every stranger on the path is called swami

Swami. A man in a black dhoti says it to the tea seller at the bottom of the hill. The tea seller says it back. A pilgrim with gray hair says it to a teenager who's stopped to catch his breath, and the teenager says it to him. On the forest path up to Sabarimala, it's how people greet each other, thank each other, ask each other to move aside. Swami: the word for a master, a holy one, the Lord, used for everyone. Today, the pilgrimage up Ayyappa's hill.

segments.voice: Tradition says that when Manikandan's work on earth was done, he shot an arrow and asked that his temple be built where it fell. It fell on a hill in the forest: Sabarimala, where Ayyappa is worshiped seated in meditation. Pilgrims don't just set out. For a season before the climb they keep a vow. They wear a bead necklace, dress in black or dark blue, eat simple food, give up alcohol and keep celibacy, and often walk barefoot. From the day the necklace goes on, the pilgrim is called swami, and even Ayyappa, by name. The vow makes the pilgrim a little like the god they're going to see. Each pilgrim climbs with the irumudi on the head, a cloth bundle tied in two parts. One part carries offerings, including a coconut filled with ghee for the god. The other carries food for the road. The forest echoes with a chant: Swamiye saranam Ayyappa, Lord, you are my refuge, Ayyappa. On the way, pilgrims stop at Erumeli, where Ayyappa's companion in the stories, a Muslim named Vavar, is honored too. Rich and poor, old and young, wear the same dark cloth, carry the same bundle, and answer to the same name. Tradition says that above the shrine are the words tat tvam asi, that thou art, from the Upanishads. Some hear it as the god speaking to the pilgrim: what you came looking for, you are.
screen: `WHERE THE ARROW FELL` · `A SEASON OF VOWS` · `THE IRUMUDI ON THE HEAD` · `THAT THOU ART`

segments.voice: Breathe in slowly, and on each out-breath take one step up a forest hill in your mind. Each time a face comes to mind, someone easy or someone hard, greet them inwardly the pilgrim's way: swami. If you pray, you can say the pilgrims' chant, Swamiye saranam Ayyappa, softly, in time with the steps.

1400.title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
1400.hook: a boy with a staff and a loincloth walks out of his village and keeps walking until he reaches Gujarat
1400.howItsDone: Swaminarayan followers tell the story of Nilkanth Varni's journey on foot across India, and their temples may show the young yogi standing on one leg in austerity, with his staff and beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa ended on the hill at Sabarimala, where every pilgrim is called swami. This week also gave us a king welcomed home with flowers, and a boy who rode home on a tigress.

Bare feet on a mountain path, high in the Himalayas. A boy, thin from fasting, wearing only a loincloth, carrying a staff, a string of beads and a small bundle. No family with him. No guide. In the stories his followers tell, he left home young, and he's been walking ever since: through snow, through forests, across rivers, from one holy place to the next, looking for something. People along the road call him Nilkanth. Today, a new region, Gujarat, and the walk that brought this boy there.
screen: `BARE FEET IN THE HIMALAYAS` → `A BOY WITH A STAFF` → `NILKANTH, WALKING`

segments.voice: Tradition says he was born Ghanshyam, in a village called Chhapaiya, not far from Ayodhya in the north. His family were devout, and he was a child who loved scripture and prayer. After his parents died, he left home as a young renunciant, a brahmachari, and took the name Nilkanth, blue-throat, one of the names of Shiva. His followers tell of a long journey on foot across India: the Himalayas, the holy sites of the east, the temples of the south. Tradition tells of him standing in hard austerities in the mountains, of meeting yogis and teachers, and of moving on from each one. He wasn't wandering for its own sake. He was asking questions and not settling for half answers. At last he comes west, into Gujarat, to a small ashram at a village called Loj. It belongs to a teacher named Ramanand Swami, and one of his disciples, Muktanand, is there to receive the young stranger. Nilkanth asks his questions: about the soul, about God, about the world and what binds us to it. And this time he stays. That's the seed of what's now called the Swaminarayan tradition, a living Hindu community with deep roots in Gujarat and temples well beyond it. A tradition that today feels rooted, organized and very much at home began with a boy who had no home at all, only a road and a question.
screen: `GHANSHYAM BECOMES NILKANTH` · `A WALK ACROSS INDIA` · `ARRIVING AT LOJ IN GUJARAT` · `A BOY WITH A ROAD AND A QUESTION`

segments.voice: Sit tall, as if you had a staff in your hand, and let a real question come up, one you haven't finished with, about God, about yourself, about what matters. Don't answer it; let it walk with you, breath after breath, the way Nilkanth carried his questions from place to place. If you pray, you can hold the question as a prayer.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, Nilkanth: the boy born Ghanshyam, who walked across India with his questions until he reached Ramanand Swami's ashram at Loj. Today's word.
